Comment: Unfortunately I wasn't able to get a photograph of this.  Pretty large Amblyscirtes - slighly larger than a nearby P. taxiles. Fairly plain with a weakly checkered fringe.  Plain brown background on the underwings with small but distinct white spots forming a "C" on a post median stripe with about three additional white spots anterior to this.  the "C" stripe wasn't exact as the  white dot at the outer point of the "C" seemed especially stretched posteriorly while the next lower spot was slanted more anteriorly than what might make a perfect "C" shape  (i.e. rather than a perfect "C" shape it looked as if it were trying to make a backwards "3" shape but without quite getting there)  No black outlines to the white dots.  NOTE:  I have never knowingly identified an A. exoteria before so I'm a bit unsure of this call, and especially within this genus, which can be a puzzling genus.  Nevertheless, unless this is some "south of the border" species" this seems to be the only Amblyscirtes that fits the description.

Location: Percha Dam State Park, Sierra County, NM, United States
Remarks: Spectacular butterflying here today - and a first state record to boot!!!
Comment: To our knowledge this is also the only state record. Unfortunately, while Rustay shot excellent video, the video was filmed on V8 and is no longer accessible. But Steve Cary did view the video and placed it on the state list as a result of this. Here's the account from Neville's field notes: "Christopher and I were puzzling out an orange Hesperia-type skipper in the milkweeds at the south end of the bosque at Percha, when Christopher spotted what he said was a giant skipper. I had barely focused my binoculars on it when it dropped straight down and out of sight. I knew, however, that it wasn't a giant skipper, per se, but rather, one of the longtail group. We eventually found it again, and it was quite tame, feeding intently on the milkweed blossoms. I thought it might be a short-tailed skipper, but the habitat listed is higher elevation oak woodlands, which this was certainly not. We grudgingly settled on silver-spotted skipper, though the pattern didn't match exactly. Eventually, Christopher went farther in the book and found the picture of zilpa longtail, a tropical species that strays to the Brownsville area and rarely to southeastern Arizona. Our butterfly was an exact match for the heavily mottled underwings, down to the bilobed black spot in front of a large white slash on the trailing edge of the underhindwing, a circular brown-rimmed spot on the costal margin of the underhindwing, and the inverted black triangle behind the underforewing apex. The only difference was that the tails had broken off a couple millimeters from the edge of the hindwing. Christopher got excellent video of it. "

Comment: New to this so I will record my thinking. Starting with a dark skipper with three small white spots on both upperside and lowerside of forewing. Also, at least two larger white spots. Candiadtes: Northern Cloudywing - white spots seem too prominent. Southern Cloudywing - white spots do not match expected pattern. Dusted Skipper - no prominent white around eyes. Also late and out of range. Female Zabulon Skipper has white edging and is out of range. Clouded Skipper lacks large white square spot and is way out of range. Female "pocahantas" form of Hobomok Skipper lacks squarish white spot. Best guess: Little Glassywing - "large square" spot is supportive.

Comment: While I watched a perched Hobomok, another perched on same leaf behind it. The first (female?) began to flutter its wings rapidly, barely unfolded, for a long time. The other moved a bit but mostly, I can see in the multiple frames, curved its abdomen around towards the perched one, probably trying to mate: Do they mate really quickly, several times in a row? Or was it rebuffed? The perched one kept wingbeating even after the other left, and another did land again, and a bit more similar behaviour occurred. Is the wing beating a signal? a pheromone dispersal? a rebuffing? Quite interesting to watch and speculate about the purpose.
